Question 1 of 20
  1. 1

    Exactly one of these four statements is true. Which one?

    Answer choices for question 1

    Solution

    Correct answer: B

    You chose A: Counts the single factor of 111 twice, once as the 111 and once as the number itself, although a prime needs two DISTINCT factors and 111 supplies one.

    You chose C: Counts the factor 222 as an extra factor of the number 222, although there it IS the number itself, so the list 1,21, 21,2 still holds only two entries.

    You chose D: Reads odd as the test for prime, although 9=3×39 = 3 \times 39=3×3 is odd and has three factors; being odd only rules out the divisor 222.

    Prime and composite are settled by a count of DISTINCT factors: exactly two makes a number prime, more than two makes it composite.

    factors of 1:  1factors of 2:  1,2factors of 9:  1,3,9\text{factors of } 1: \; 1 \qquad \text{factors of } 2: \; 1, 2 \qquad \text{factors of } 9: \; 1, 3, 9factors of 1:1factors of 2:1,2factors of 9:1,3,9

    The list for 111 holds one number, which is neither exactly two nor more than two, so 111 meets neither definition. The number 222 has exactly two factors and is prime, its evenness costing it nothing because the factor 222 is the number itself rather than a third factor. And 999 is odd with three factors, so odd numbers can be composite.

  2. 2

    Which of these four numbers is divisible by 999?

    Answer choices for question 2

    Solution

    Correct answer: C

    You chose A: Stops once the digit sum 151515 is seen to be a multiple of 333, although the test for 999 asks for a digit sum that is a multiple of 999.

    You chose B: Looks for a digit 999 inside the numeral instead of adding the digits, which here give 161616.

    You chose D: Reads the last digit, as the tests for 222, 555 and 101010 do, and accepts a numeral ending in 999; the digit sum is 171717.

    Every place value is one more than a multiple of 999, so each column hands over a multiple of 999 and leaves one copy of its digit behind. Adding the digits collects those leftovers, and the verdict rests on that sum.

    5+3+8+2=18=9×25 + 3 + 8 + 2 = 18 = 9 \times 25+3+8+2=18=9×2

    So 5,3825{,}3825,382 is divisible by 999, and dividing confirms it: 5,382=9×5985{,}382 = 9 \times 5985,382=9×598. The other three give digit sums 151515, 161616 and 171717, and none of those is a multiple of 999.

  3. 3

    Which of these is the prime factorization of 968968968?

    Answer choices for question 3

    Solution

    Correct answer: A

    You chose B: Stops while 121121121 is still composite; it is odd, its digits add to 444 and it does not end in 000 or 555, but 121=11×11121 = 11 \times 11121=11×11.

    You chose C: Stops dividing by 222 while the quotient 242242242 is still even, so one copy of 222 is missing and the product comes to 484484484.

    You chose D: Counts one copy of 111111 although dividing 121121121 by 111111 leaves 111111 again, so the product comes to 888888.

    Divide by the smallest prime that fits at each step. The number is even three times over.

    968÷2=484,484÷2=242,242÷2=121968 \div 2 = 484, \quad 484 \div 2 = 242, \quad 242 \div 2 = 121968÷2=484,484÷2=242,242÷2=121

    Now 121121121 is odd and its digits add to 444, so 222 and 333 are finished, and it does not end in 000 or 555. The next prime that fits is 111111, and 121÷11=11121 \div 11 = 11121÷11=11, which is prime.

    968=2×2×2×11×11=23×112968 = 2 \times 2 \times 2 \times 11 \times 11 = 2^3 \times 11^2968=2×2×2×11×11=23×112

  4. 4

    What is GCF⁡(75,120)\operatorname{GCF}(75, 120)GCF(75,120)?

    Answer choices for question 4

    Solution

    Correct answer: D

    You chose A: Takes the highest power of each shared prime instead of the lowest, asking for 3×523 \times 5^23×52, although 120120120 owns only one copy of 555.

    You chose B: Takes the highest power of every prime in either number, which builds the least common multiple 23×3×522^3 \times 3 \times 5^223×3×52 rather than a common factor.

    You chose C: Keeps only the shared prime 555 and drops the shared 333, although both numbers own a copy of each.

    Write each number in prime-power form and go prime by prime.

    75=3×52,120=23×3×575 = 3 \times 5^2, \qquad 120 = 2^3 \times 3 \times 575=3×52,120=23×3×5

    A common factor can carry no more copies of a prime than the number that owns fewer, so take the lowest power of each SHARED prime. The prime 222 is missing from 757575 and drops out; the prime 333 appears once in each; the prime 555 appears twice in 757575 but once in 120120120.

    GCF⁡(75,120)=3×5=15\operatorname{GCF}(75, 120) = 3 \times 5 = 15GCF(75,120)=3×5=15

    As a check, 75÷15=575 \div 15 = 575÷15=5 and 120÷15=8120 \div 15 = 8120÷15=8, both whole.

  5. 5

    Exactly one of these four numbers is divisible by 444 and not by 888. Which one?

    Answer choices for question 5

    Solution

    Correct answer: C

    You chose A: Runs the test for 888 on the last two digits, and 525252 is not a multiple of 888, although that test reads the last three: 352=8×44352 = 8 \times 44352=8×44.

    You chose B: Accepts an even last digit as divisibility by 444, although that test reads the number made by the last two digits, and 464646 is not a multiple of 444.

    You chose D: Adds the digits to test for 888, as the tests for 333 and 999 do, and 6+4+8+8=266 + 4 + 8 + 8 = 266+4+8+8=26 is not a multiple of 888, although 488=8×61488 = 8 \times 61488=8×61.

    The test for 444 reads the number made by the last two digits, because 100=4×25100 = 4 \times 25100=4×25; the test for 888 reads the last three, because 1000=8×1251000 = 8 \times 1251000=8×125.

    24=4×6,124=(8×15)+424 = 4 \times 6, \qquad 124 = (8 \times 15) + 424=4×6,124=(8×15)+4

    So 5,1245{,}1245,124 clears the first test and fails the second. Of the others, 2,9462{,}9462,946 fails the test for 444 already, since 464646 is not a multiple of 444, while 7,3527{,}3527,352 and 6,4886{,}4886,488 pass both tests, because 352=8×44352 = 8 \times 44352=8×44 and 488=8×61488 = 8 \times 61488=8×61.

  6. 6

    Exactly one of these four numbers is prime. Which one?

    Answer choices for question 6

    Solution

    Correct answer: B

    You chose A: Overlooks the last digit; a number ending in 555 is a multiple of 555, and 355=5×71355 = 5 \times 71355=5×71.

    You chose C: Declares the number prime once 222, 333 and 555 have all failed, although the search still owes 777, and 371=7×53371 = 7 \times 53371=7×53.

    You chose D: Misses the digit sum 151515, a multiple of 333, so the number is taken to have no small divisor, although 357=3×119357 = 3 \times 119357=3×119.

    Screen with the quick tests first, then divide.

    355=5×71,357=3×119,371=7×53355 = 5 \times 71, \qquad 357 = 3 \times 119, \qquad 371 = 7 \times 53355=5×71,357=3×119,371=7×53

    That leaves 349349349. It is odd, its digit sum 161616 is not a multiple of 333, and it does not end in 000 or 555. Dividing by 777, 111111, 131313 and 171717 leaves a remainder every time, and the next candidate is 191919, where 19×19=36119 \times 19 = 36119×19=361 has already passed 349349349. There is no factor pair left to find, so 349349349 is prime.

  7. 7

    A club has 102102102 badges of one colour and 170170170 of another. They are to be made up into identical packs, each pack holding the same number of each colour with none left over, and there are to be as many packs as possible. How many packs are there?

    Answer choices for question 7

    Solution

    Correct answer: A

    You chose B: Takes the highest power of every prime, which gives the smallest number both totals divide into rather than the largest number that divides both.

    You chose C: Keeps only the shared prime 171717 and drops the shared 222, so the count of packs comes out half of what it could be.

    You chose D: Adds the two per-pack counts, 333 of one colour and 555 of the other, reporting the size of a pack rather than the number of packs.

    Every pack takes an equal share of each colour, so the number of packs divides both totals, and as many packs as possible means the greatest of those common divisors.

    102=2×3×17,170=2×5×17102 = 2 \times 3 \times 17, \qquad 170 = 2 \times 5 \times 17102=2×3×17,170=2×5×17

    The primes shared by both are 222 and 171717, each appearing once in each number.

    GCF⁡(102,170)=2×17=34\operatorname{GCF}(102, 170) = 2 \times 17 = 34GCF(102,170)=2×17=34

    So there are 343434 packs, each holding 102÷34=3102 \div 34 = 3102÷34=3 badges of the first colour and 170÷34=5170 \div 34 = 5170÷34=5 of the second.

  8. 8

    One factor tree for 468468468 ends with the leaves 222, 222, 333, 333 and 131313. Another ends with the leaves 222, 999, 222 and 131313. Which statement is true?

    Answer choices for question 8

    Solution

    Correct answer: D

    You chose A: Reads a mismatch as evidence that the route matters, although a list still holding a composite is not a finished tree to compare with.

    You chose B: Counts a product containing the composite 999 as a prime factorization, although every factor written in one has to be prime.

    You chose C: Takes a two-digit leaf to be composite because it is the largest one there, although the only factors of 131313 are 111 and 131313.

    A tree is finished exactly when every leaf is prime. In the second list the leaf 999 is not: its digits add to 999, so 333 divides it.

    9=3×3,2×9×2×13=4689 = 3 \times 3, \qquad 2 \times 9 \times 2 \times 13 = 4689=3×3,2×9×2×13=468

    Splitting that leaf turns the second list into 222, 333, 333, 222, 131313, which is the first list in a different order.

    468=22×32×13468 = 2^2 \times 3^2 \times 13468=22×32×13

    A whole number greater than 111 has one prime factorization apart from the order of its factors, so two finished trees can never disagree. Where a mismatch shows up, one of the trees has been stopped a branch early, which is exactly what the leaf 999 records here.

  9. 9

    Why does the test for 888 read the last three digits of a number and no more?

    Answer choices for question 9

    Solution

    Correct answer: A

    You chose B: Passes the one-digit test for 222 up to 888, although 121212 is even and is not a multiple of 888; a factor of the divisor does not bring its own test with it.

    You chose C: Transfers the digit-sum rule from 333 and 999 to 888, although 161616 is a multiple of 888 and its digits add to 777.

    You chose D: Combines two tests whose divisors share a factor of 222, so that factor is counted twice; 121212 passes both and is not a multiple of 888.

    Split the number at the thousands column, into the part built from thousands and above and the number made by the last three digits.

    N=(1000×m)+L,1000=8×125N = (1000 \times m) + L, \qquad 1000 = 8 \times 125N=(1000×m)+L,1000=8×125

    The first piece is 8×125×m8 \times 125 \times m8×125×m whatever mmm is, so it leaves remainder 000 and cannot affect the verdict. The whole question therefore rests on LLL, the last three digits. The same split one column earlier, where 100=4×25100 = 4 \times 25100=4×25, is why the test for 444 needs only two digits.

  10. 10

    For 565656 and 707070 the greatest common factor is 141414. What is LCM⁡(56,70)\operatorname{LCM}(56, 70)LCM(56,70)?

    Answer choices for question 10

    Solution

    Correct answer: C

    You chose A: Uses the plain product 56×7056 \times 7056×70, which is a common multiple but the least one only when the two numbers share no prime.

    You chose B: Reports the greatest common factor again, although a common multiple can never be smaller than either number.

    You chose D: Takes the larger of the two numbers, as though the least common multiple were always the larger one, although 707070 is not a multiple of 565656.

    For two numbers, the greatest common factor and the least common multiple take the lower and the higher power of every prime, which is that pair of counts over again, so together they multiply back to the numbers multiplied together.

    GCF⁡(56,70)×LCM⁡(56,70)=56×70=3,920\operatorname{GCF}(56, 70) \times \operatorname{LCM}(56, 70) = 56 \times 70 = 3{,}920GCF(56,70)×LCM(56,70)=56×70=3,920

    Dividing the product by the greatest common factor leaves the least common multiple.

    LCM⁡(56,70)=3,920÷14=280\operatorname{LCM}(56, 70) = 3{,}920 \div 14 = 280LCM(56,70)=3,920÷14=280

    The prime powers agree: 56=23×756 = 2^3 \times 756=23×7 and 70=2×5×770 = 2 \times 5 \times 770=2×5×7, so the highest powers give 23×5×7=2802^3 \times 5 \times 7 = 28023×5×7=280.

  11. 11

    What is LCM⁡(18,30,50)\operatorname{LCM}(18, 30, 50)LCM(18,30,50)?

    Answer choices for question 11

    Solution

    Correct answer: D

    You chose A: Stops after the first two numbers; 909090 is the least common multiple of 181818 and 303030 alone, and 505050 does not divide it.

    You chose B: Multiplies in the copy of 555 from 303030 as well as the two from 505050, instead of taking the highest power of 555 that any one number holds.

    You chose C: Multiplies the three numbers together, which is a common multiple but far from the least.

    Write all three in prime-power form and take the highest power of every prime that appears anywhere, because a common multiple must hold enough copies for each number on its own.

    18=2×32,30=2×3×5,50=2×5218 = 2 \times 3^2, \qquad 30 = 2 \times 3 \times 5, \qquad 50 = 2 \times 5^218=2×32,30=2×3×5,50=2×52

    The most copies of 222 any one of them holds is one, the most copies of 333 is two, in 181818, and the most copies of 555 is two, in 505050.

    LCM⁡(18,30,50)=2×32×52=450\operatorname{LCM}(18, 30, 50) = 2 \times 3^2 \times 5^2 = 450LCM(18,30,50)=2×32×52=450

    Each number divides it: 450÷18=25450 \div 18 = 25450÷18=25, 450÷30=15450 \div 30 = 15450÷30=15 and 450÷50=9450 \div 50 = 9450÷50=9.

  12. 12

    Exactly one of these four combined tests is sound. Which one?

    Answer choices for question 12

    Solution

    Correct answer: C

    You chose A: Multiplies 222 by 888 although the two share a factor of 222, so that factor is counted twice; 242424 passes both tests and is not a multiple of 161616.

    You chose B: Multiplies 333 by 666 although the test for 666 already contains the test for 333, so nothing new is added; 121212 passes both and is not a multiple of 181818.

    You chose D: Multiplies 444 by 101010 although the two share a factor of 222; 202020 passes both tests and is not a multiple of 404040.

    Passing two tests puts both divisors inside the number, but it delivers their product only when the two share no factor above 111. Otherwise the shared part is counted twice and the claim overshoots.

    5×9=45,5 and 9 share no factor above 15 \times 9 = 45, \qquad 5 \text{ and } 9 \text{ share no factor above } 15×9=45,5 and 9 share no factor above 1

    So a number carrying a factor 555 and a factor 999 carries them without overlap and is a multiple of 454545, and every multiple of 454545 passes both tests, which is the other direction. Each of the other three pairings shares a factor: 242424 passes the tests for 222 and 888, 121212 passes the tests for 333 and 666, and 202020 passes the tests for 444 and 101010, yet none of the three is a multiple of the product claimed.

  13. 13

    The number 493493493 is odd, its digits add to 161616, and it does not end in 000 or 555, so it fails the tests for 222, 333, 444, 555, 666, 888, 999 and 101010. What follows?

    Answer choices for question 13

    Solution

    Correct answer: C

    You chose A: Reads the failed tests as ruling out every divisor, although they rule out only the ones they name; the search still owes 777, 111111, 131313, 171717 and 191919.

    You chose B: Overlooks the stopping rule, which ends the search once a candidate times itself passes 493493493, and that happens at 232323.

    You chose D: Assumes every composite number has a divisor of 101010 or less, although this one's smallest divisor above 111 is 171717.

    The failed tests rule out the divisors they name and nothing more. The search still owes every prime whose square does not pass 493493493, which runs 777, 111111, 131313, 171717 and 191919, since 19×19=36119 \times 19 = 36119×19=361 is below 493493493 while 23×23=52923 \times 23 = 52923×23=529 is above it.

    493÷17=29,so 493=17×29493 \div 17 = 29, \qquad \text{so } 493 = 17 \times 29493÷17=29,so 493=17×29

    The divisions by 777, 111111 and 131313 each leave a remainder, but 171717 goes in exactly, so a third factor exists and the number is composite. Failing every taught test is not the same as being prime: those tests reach only as far as 101010.

  14. 14

    A workshop runs a deep clean every 151515 days and a stock count every 404040 days, and both happen today. How many days pass before they next fall on the same day?

    Answer choices for question 14

    Solution

    Correct answer: A

    You chose B: Reports how many deep cleans happen in that time rather than the number of days the question asks for.

    You chose C: Takes the lowest power of the shared prime, which gives the largest interval dividing both cycles rather than the first day the two meet.

    You chose D: Multiplies the two cycle lengths, which is a day both cycles do land on, but not the first such day.

    Each job falls on the multiples of its own cycle, so they coincide on a common multiple and NEXT coincide on the smallest one.

    15=3×5,40=23×515 = 3 \times 5, \qquad 40 = 2^3 \times 515=3×5,40=23×5

    Take the highest power of every prime that appears in either.

    LCM⁡(15,40)=23×3×5=120\operatorname{LCM}(15, 40) = 2^3 \times 3 \times 5 = 120LCM(15,40)=23×3×5=120

    So 120120120 days pass, which is 120÷15=8120 \div 15 = 8120÷15=8 deep cleans and 120÷40=3120 \div 40 = 3120÷40=3 stock counts, both whole counts as they must be.

  15. 15

    What is the prime factorization of 1,1761{,}1761,176?

    Answer choices for question 15

    Solution

    Correct answer: D

    You chose A: Stops while 494949 is still composite, although 49=7×749 = 7 \times 749=7×7 and a factorization may hold nothing but primes.

    You chose B: Stops dividing by 222 while the quotient 294294294 is still even, so one copy of 222 is lost and the product comes to 588588588.

    You chose C: Counts one copy of 777 although the quotient 494949 holds two of them, so the product comes to 168168168.

    Divide by the smallest prime that fits, over and over, until the quotient reaches 111.

    1,176÷2=588,588÷2=294,294÷2=1471{,}176 \div 2 = 588, \quad 588 \div 2 = 294, \quad 294 \div 2 = 1471,176÷2=588,588÷2=294,294÷2=147

    Now 147147147 is odd, so 222 is finished, and its digits add to 121212, so 333 fits: 147÷3=49147 \div 3 = 49147÷3=49. The quotient 494949 is 7×77 \times 77×7, and dividing twice by 777 reaches 111.

    1,176=23×3×721{,}176 = 2^3 \times 3 \times 7^21,176=23×3×72

    Multiplying back, 8×3×49=1,1768 \times 3 \times 49 = 1{,}1768×3×49=1,176.

  16. 16

    For a=22×52a = 2^2 \times 5^2a=22×52 and b=23×5×7b = 2^3 \times 5 \times 7b=23×5×7, what is GCF⁡(a,b)×LCM⁡(a,b)\operatorname{GCF}(a, b) \times \operatorname{LCM}(a, b)GCF(a,b)×LCM(a,b)?

    Answer choices for question 16

    Solution

    Correct answer: B

    You chose A: Adds the two answers instead of multiplying them.

    You chose C: Divides the least common multiple by the greatest common factor, as though one of the answers were contained in the other.

    You chose D: Reports the least common multiple on its own, which would be the whole product only if the greatest common factor were 111.

    Take the lowest power of each shared prime for one answer and the highest power of every prime for the other.

    GCF⁡(a,b)=22×5=20,LCM⁡(a,b)=23×52×7=1,400\operatorname{GCF}(a, b) = 2^2 \times 5 = 20, \qquad \operatorname{LCM}(a, b) = 2^3 \times 5^2 \times 7 = 1{,}400GCF(a,b)=22×5=20,LCM(a,b)=23×52×7=1,400

    Multiplying them gives 20×1,400=28,00020 \times 1{,}400 = 28{,}00020×1,400=28,000. Between them the two answers take the lower and the higher count of every prime, which is the pair of counts over again, so the result has to be aaa times bbb.

    a×b=100×280=28,000a \times b = 100 \times 280 = 28{,}000a×b=100×280=28,000

  17. 17

    What makes the digit sum decide divisibility by 999?

    Answer choices for question 17

    Solution

    Correct answer: B

    You chose A: Attaches the rule to the column value itself; 726726726 leaves 666 on division by 101010 while its digit sum 151515 leaves 555.

    You chose C: Treats every smaller number made from the digits as inheriting the divisibility, although 727272 is also built from the digits of 726726726 and is a multiple of 999, while 726726726 is not.

    You chose D: Runs the digit-sum test for 333 a second time on the digit sum, although 333333 passes that twice over and is not a multiple of 999.

    Every place value sits one above a string of nines.

    10=9+1,100=99+1,1000=999+110 = 9 + 1, \qquad 100 = 99 + 1, \qquad 1000 = 999 + 110=9+1,100=99+1,1000=999+1

    A digit bbb in the tens column therefore contributes b×10=(b×9)+bb \times 10 = (b \times 9) + bb×10=(b×9)+b: a multiple of 999, and one loose copy of bbb. Every column behaves that way, so the number is a multiple of 999 plus the sum of its digits, and only that sum can decide the verdict.

    726=(7×99)+(2×9)+(7+2+6)726 = (7 \times 99) + (2 \times 9) + (7 + 2 + 6)726=(7×99)+(2×9)+(7+2+6)

    Here the digit sum is 151515, which is not a multiple of 999, so 726726726 is not either, although it is a multiple of 333.

  18. 18

    Exactly one of these four statements is true. Which one?

    Answer choices for question 18

    Solution

    Correct answer: A

    You chose B: Reads the same primes as the same factorization, although the counts may differ: 20=22×520 = 2^2 \times 520=22×5 and 50=2×5250 = 2 \times 5^250=2×52 are built from 222 and 555 alone.

    You chose C: Extends the theorem below the range it states; 111 is not prime, so 111 standing alone is not a product of primes, which is why the statement begins at 222.

    You chose D: Counts two orderings of the same primes as two factorizations, although the theorem sets order aside and 2×3×72 \times 3 \times 72×3×7 and 7×3×27 \times 3 \times 27×3×2 are one factorization written twice.

    Every whole number greater than 111 has exactly one prime factorization, apart from the order in which the factors are written. Two numbers with the same factorization are therefore the same product, and so the same number.

    22×5=20,2×52=502^2 \times 5 = 20, \qquad 2 \times 5^2 = 5022×5=20,2×52=50

    Those two are built from the same primes and are not equal, so sharing the primes is not enough: the COUNTS have to match as well. Order, by contrast, is set aside by the theorem, so 2×3×72 \times 3 \times 72×3×7 and 7×3×27 \times 3 \times 27×3×2 are one factorization. And the theorem starts at 222, because 111 is not prime and so is not a product of primes at all.

  19. 19

    For which of these sets of three whole numbers does the greatest common factor times the least common multiple equal the three numbers multiplied together?

    Answer choices for question 19

    Solution

    Correct answer: D

    You chose A: Reads a greatest common factor of 111 as enough, although 101010 shares a prime with each of the others: the two answers give 1×10=101 \times 10 = 101×10=10 while the product is 100100100.

    You chose B: Reads no factor common to all three as no sharing at all, although each PAIR shares a prime: the two answers give 1×30=301 \times 30 = 301×30=30 while the product is 900900900.

    You chose C: Carries the two-number rule to three, although the middle count of each prime is collected by neither answer: the two answers give 3×12=363 \times 12 = 363×12=36 while the product is 216216216.

    The rule for two numbers works because a pair of counts holds nothing but a lower one and a higher one, so the two answers use the pair up. A third number brings a middle count that neither answer ever reaches for, so the rule survives only when there is nothing in the middle to lose, and that happens when no two of the three share a prime.

    4=22,9=32,25=524 = 2^2, \qquad 9 = 3^2, \qquad 25 = 5^24=22,9=32,25=52

    No prime appears in more than one of them, so the greatest common factor is 111 and the least common multiple is everything at once.

    1×(22×32×52)=900=4×9×251 \times (2^2 \times 3^2 \times 5^2) = 900 = 4 \times 9 \times 251×(22×32×52)=900=4×9×25

    In each of the other three sets some prime is held by two of the numbers, and the copies in the middle go uncounted.

  20. 20

    What is the prime factorization of 2,8602{,}8602,860?

    Answer choices for question 20

    Solution

    Correct answer: B

    You chose A: Divides by 222 only once although the quotient 1,4301{,}4301,430 is still even, so the product comes to 1,4301{,}4301,430.

    You chose C: Stops while 143143143 is still composite; it fails the tests for 222, 333, 555 and 999, but 143=11×13143 = 11 \times 13143=11×13.

    You chose D: Leaves the composite 444 standing as a base, although a prime-power form has only primes as bases and 4=224 = 2^24=22.

    Peel off the small primes first. The number is even, and even again once halved, and the next quotient ends in 555.

    2,860÷2=1,430,1,430÷2=715,715÷5=1432{,}860 \div 2 = 1{,}430, \quad 1{,}430 \div 2 = 715, \quad 715 \div 5 = 1432,860÷2=1,430,1,430÷2=715,715÷5=143

    Now 143143143 is odd, its digits add to 888 and it does not end in 000 or 555, so those tests all fail and the search moves up. Dividing by 777 leaves a remainder, and dividing by 111111 does not: 143÷11=13143 \div 11 = 13143÷11=13, which is prime.

    2,860=22×5×11×132{,}860 = 2^2 \times 5 \times 11 \times 132,860=22×5×11×13

    1. One numeral, five tests . 11 points. Question 1 of 10.

    11 pts

    A single whole number can be put past several divisibility tests in one pass, and each test reads a different part of the numeral: some read one digit, some read a block of digits, and some read every digit there is.

    1. A
      Part A.

      Decide which of 222, 444, 555, 888 and 101010 divide 7,4167{,}4167,416, and say for each test which part of the numeral it reads.

      Solve and show your work Write each step out, and end with the value and its units. 3 points

    2. B
      Part B.

      The four-digit number 6,3□06{,}3\square 06,3□0 has one digit missing. Give every digit that makes it divisible by 999, every digit that makes it divisible by 444, and every digit that does both.

      Solve and show your work Write each step out, and end with the value and its units. 3 points

    3. C
      Part C.

      A student writes: "7,4167{,}4167,416 is divisible by 888, because its last two digits form 161616 and 161616 is a multiple of 888." Decide whether the verdict is right, decide whether the reasoning is right, and give a four-digit number on which the student's rule and the true verdict disagree, if one exists.

      Carry your own answer forward Judge the student's verdict against your own answer for 7,4167{,}4167,416 in part A, whatever it came to.

      Find and correct the error Say which line first goes wrong, why it is wrong, and then do it correctly. 5 points

    The answer

    Part A

    222, 444 and 888 divide 7,4167{,}4167,416; 555 and 101010 do not. The tests for 222, 555 and 101010 read the last digit, the test for 444 the last two digits, and the test for 888 the last three.

    Part B

    For 999 the digit is 000 or 999. For 444 it is 000, 222, 444, 666 or 888. Only 000 does both.

    Part C

    The verdict is right, since 7,416=8×9277{,}416 = 8 \times 9277,416=8×927, but the reasoning is not: the test for 888 reads the last three digits, because 100010001000 is a multiple of 888 while 100100100 is not. The same reasoning passes 2,9322{,}9322,932, whose last two digits give 323232, and 2,9322{,}9322,932 is not a multiple of 888.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    Three of the tests read the last digit alone, because every column above the ones is built from tens. The last digit here is 666, which is even, so 222 divides the number, while 555 and 101010 need a last digit of 000 or 555 and do not get one.

    7,416=(741×10)+67{,}416 = (741 \times 10) + 67,416=(741×10)+6

    The test for 444 reads one column further in, since 100=4×25100 = 4 \times 25100=4×25 makes everything above the last two digits a multiple of 444. The test for 888 reads one further still, since 1000=8×1251000 = 8 \times 1251000=8×125.

    16=4×4,416=8×5216 = 4 \times 4, \qquad 416 = 8 \times 5216=4×4,416=8×52

    Both of those leftovers are clean, so 444 and 888 divide 7,4167{,}4167,416 as well.

    Part B

    For 999, add the digits and set the sum against the multiples of 999. The known digits give 6+3+0=96 + 3 + 0 = 96+3+0=9, so the blank digit ddd has to make 9+d9 + d9+d a multiple of 999.

    9+d=9⇒d=0,9+d=18⇒d=99 + d = 9 \Rightarrow d = 0, \qquad 9 + d = 18 \Rightarrow d = 99+d=9⇒d=0,9+d=18⇒d=9

    For 444, only the last two digits matter, and they read ddd then 000, which is the number 10×d10 \times d10×d. Run through the ten digits and pick out the two-digit numbers that are multiples of 444.

    00,  20,  40,  60,  80 are multiples of 4;10,  30,  50,  70,  90 are not00, \; 20, \; 40, \; 60, \; 80 \text{ are multiples of } 4; \qquad 10, \; 30, \; 50, \; 70, \; 90 \text{ are not}00,20,40,60,80 are multiples of 4;10,30,50,70,90 are not

    So the even digits pass the test for 444. The only digit on both lists is 000, giving 6,3006{,}3006,300, which is 9×7009 \times 7009×700 and 4×1,5754 \times 1{,}5754×1,575.

    Part C

    Take the two questions apart. The verdict happens to be right, and dividing settles that.

    7,416=8×9277{,}416 = 8 \times 9277,416=8×927

    The reasoning is still wrong, and the place-value split shows why. Splitting at the hundreds column leaves a piece that is a multiple of 100100100, and 100100100 is not a multiple of 888: it is 8×12+48 \times 12 + 48×12+4. So the hundreds column can still carry a remainder into the answer, and the last two digits cannot settle the question on their own. Splitting one column further out fixes it, because 1000=8×1251000 = 8 \times 1251000=8×125.

    A number where the student's rule breaks is one whose last two digits form a multiple of 888 while the last three do not.

    2,932:32=8×4,932=(8×116)+42{,}932: \quad 32 = 8 \times 4, \qquad 932 = (8 \times 116) + 42,932:32=8×4,932=(8×116)+4

    The student's rule calls 2,9322{,}9322,932 divisible by 888, and it is not.

    In one line

    Of 222, 444, 555, 888 and 101010, the divisors of 7,4167{,}4167,416 are 222, 444 and 888, found by reading the last digit, the last two digits and the last three digits. In 6,3□06{,}3\square 06,3□0 the blank must be 000 or 999 for divisibility by 999 and any even digit for divisibility by 444, so only 000 does both. The student's verdict on 7,4167{,}4167,416 is right and the reasoning is not: the test for 888 reads three digits, not two, and on 2,9322{,}9322,932 the same reasoning gives the wrong answer.

    2. What the factor count decides . 12 points. Question 2 of 10.

    12 pts

    Prime and composite are settled by a count and nothing else: how many distinct whole numbers divide the number leaving no remainder. Exactly two makes it prime, more than two makes it composite.

    1. A
      Part A.

      List every factor of 929292 and every factor of 301301301. Give each count, and classify each number.

      Solve and show your work Write each step out, and end with the value and its units. 4 points

    2. B
      Part B.

      Do the same for 111 and for 222: list every factor of each, give the counts, and classify each number by the same rule.

      Solve and show your work Write each step out, and end with the value and its units. 3 points

    3. C
      Part C.

      A classmate offers a shorter rule: a whole number is prime exactly when no whole number below it divides it except 111, and composite exactly when it is even or ends in 555. Test each half of that rule against the four numbers above, and say for each half whether it is sound, correcting anything it gets wrong.

      Carry your own answer forward Test the classmate's rule against the four numbers you classified in parts A and B, whatever you decided about each.

      Justify your claim State the claim, then give the reason it has to be true. 5 points

    The answer

    Part A

    929292 has six factors: 111, 222, 444, 232323, 464646, 929292. 301301301 has four: 111, 777, 434343, 301301301. Both counts pass two, so both numbers are composite.

    Part B

    111 has one factor, 111 itself, so it is neither prime nor composite. 222 has two factors, 111 and 222, so it is prime.

    Part C

    Both halves fail. The first calls 111 prime, since no whole number below 111 divides it, although its single factor puts it outside both groups. The second calls 222 composite although 222 is prime, and it misses 301301301, which is odd, does not end in 555, and is 7×437 \times 437×43.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    Work up through the candidate divisors, taking each factor together with its partner. For 929292, the tests for 222 and 444 both pass, and 92÷2=4692 \div 2 = 4692÷2=46, 92÷4=2392 \div 4 = 2392÷4=23.

    92=1×92=2×46=4×2392 = 1 \times 92 = 2 \times 46 = 4 \times 2392=1×92=2×46=4×23

    The candidates 555, 666, 777, 888 and 999 each leave a remainder, and 10×10=10010 \times 10 = 10010×10=100 has passed 929292, so no factor pair is left to find and the list is complete: 1,2,4,23,46,921, 2, 4, 23, 46, 921,2,4,23,46,92, six factors in all.

    For 301301301 the quick tests fail, since it is odd, its digits add to 444 and it does not end in 000 or 555. The next candidate is 777.

    301=7×43301 = 7 \times 43301=7×43

    That gives the factor list 1,7,43,3011, 7, 43, 3011,7,43,301, four factors. Six and four are both more than two, so each number is composite.

    Part B

    A factor of 111 is a whole number dividing 111 with no remainder, and only 111 does, since anything larger leaves a remainder. The "111" and the "itself" are the same number here, so they are one entry, not two.

    factors of 1:  1factors of 2:  1, 2\text{factors of } 1: \; 1 \qquad \text{factors of } 2: \; 1, \, 2factors of 1:1factors of 2:1,2

    One factor is neither exactly two nor more than two, so 111 meets neither definition and stands outside both groups. The number 222 has exactly two distinct factors, so it is prime, and it stays prime although it is even: the factor 222 is the number itself, not a third factor.

    Part C

    Take the halves one at a time, and test both directions of each.

    The first half agrees with the definition for every number greater than 111, but it says nothing about how many factors there are, so it slips at the bottom of the list. No whole number below 111 divides 111 at all, so the classmate's rule calls 111 prime.

    factors of 1:  1(one factor, so neither prime nor composite)\text{factors of } 1: \; 1 \quad \text{(one factor, so neither prime nor composite)}factors of 1:1(one factor, so neither prime nor composite)

    The second half fails in both directions at once. Going one way, 222 is even, so the rule calls it composite, and 222 is prime. Going the other way, a composite need not be even and need not end in 555.

    301=7×43301 = 7 \times 43301=7×43

    That number is odd and does not end in 555, so the rule's second half never reaches it and a composite slips straight through. Being even or ending in 555 is a quick way to CATCH some composites, never a definition of one: it names two divisors out of all there are.

    In one line

    929292 has the six factors 1,2,4,23,46,921, 2, 4, 23, 46, 921,2,4,23,46,92 and 301301301 has the four factors 1,7,43,3011, 7, 43, 3011,7,43,301, so both are composite; 111 has a single factor and is neither prime nor composite, while 222 has exactly two and is prime. The classmate's shorter rule fails at both halves: the first calls 111 prime, and the second calls the prime 222 composite while letting the composite 301=7×43301 = 7 \times 43301=7×43 through, since being even or ending in 555 names only two of the divisors a number might have.

    3. A tree and a column . 12 points. Question 3 of 10.

    12 pts

    A factor tree splits a number in whatever way you notice first and branches out; repeated division works down a single column, always taking the smallest prime that fits. Both stop for the same reason.

    1. A
      Part A.

      Build a factor tree for 588588588, taking 588=12×49588 = 12 \times 49588=12×49 as the first split. Carry every branch as far as it will go, then give the factorization in prime-power form.

      Write the expression An equation or an expression is enough here. Show how you built it. 3 points

    2. B
      Part B.

      Find the prime factorization of 1,4521{,}4521,452 by repeated division, taking the smallest prime that fits at every step, and name the test that told you each divisor would fit.

      Write the expression An equation or an expression is enough here. Show how you built it. 4 points

    3. C
      Part C.

      Say how you can tell a factor tree has gone as far as it can without multiplying anything back, and say what the small raised number in a prime-power form counts. Then decide whether 22×25×112^2 \times 25 \times 1122×25×11 is a prime factorization of 1,1001{,}1001,100, and repair it if it is not.

      Carry your own answer forward Judge that form by the same standard you applied to your own tree in part A.

      Explain why it works A sentence or two. Reasons, not steps. 5 points

    The answer

    Part A

    588=2×2×3×7×7=22×3×72588 = 2 \times 2 \times 3 \times 7 \times 7 = 2^2 \times 3 \times 7^2588=2×2×3×7×7=22×3×72.

    Part B

    1,452=22×3×1121{,}452 = 2^2 \times 3 \times 11^21,452=22×3×112, from the divisors 222, 222, 333, 111111, 111111: an even last digit for each 222, the digit sum 121212 for the 333, and division for each 111111.

    Part C

    A tree is finished when every leaf is prime, since only a composite can be split again. The raised number counts copies of that prime. The form 22×25×112^2 \times 25 \times 1122×25×11 multiplies back to 1,1001{,}1001,100, but 25=5225 = 5^225=52 is composite, so repaired it reads 22×52×112^2 \times 5^2 \times 1122×52×11.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    Neither 121212 nor 494949 is prime, so each branch splits again. The 121212 goes to 4×34 \times 34×3 and then the 444 goes to 2×22 \times 22×2; the 494949 goes to 7×77 \times 77×7.

    588=12×49=(2×2×3)×(7×7)588 = 12 \times 49 = (2 \times 2 \times 3) \times (7 \times 7)588=12×49=(2×2×3)×(7×7)

    Every leaf is now prime, so the tree is finished. Collecting the repeats into powers and listing the primes from smallest to largest,

    588=22×3×72588 = 2^2 \times 3 \times 7^2588=22×3×72

    and multiplying back gives 4×3×49=5884 \times 3 \times 49 = 5884×3×49=588.

    Part B

    The last digit is even, so 222 fits, and the quotient is even again.

    1,452÷2=726,726÷2=3631{,}452 \div 2 = 726, \qquad 726 \div 2 = 3631,452÷2=726,726÷2=363

    Now 363363363 is odd, so 222 is finished. Its digits add to 121212, a multiple of 333, so 333 fits.

    363÷3=121363 \div 3 = 121363÷3=121

    The quotient 121121121 is odd, its digits add to 444 and it does not end in 000 or 555, so 333 and 555 are out; 777 leaves a remainder, and 111111 divides it exactly, twice over.

    121÷11=11,11÷11=1121 \div 11 = 11, \qquad 11 \div 11 = 1121÷11=11,11÷11=1

    The quotient has reached 111, so the divisors used are the factorization: 1,452=22×3×1121{,}452 = 2^2 \times 3 \times 11^21,452=22×3×112.

    Part C

    The stopping condition is read off the leaves, not off a multiplication. A composite number has a factor other than 111 and itself, so it can always be split again; a prime has none, so it cannot. A tree is therefore finished exactly when every leaf is prime, and no check by multiplication is needed to see it.

    The raised number is shorthand for repeated multiplication, and it counts copies of the base.

    52=5×5=25,22=2×2=45^2 = 5 \times 5 = 25, \qquad 2^2 = 2 \times 2 = 452=5×5=25,22=2×2=4

    So it says how many times the prime appears, never what the prime is multiplied by.

    Now test the form offered. Its arithmetic is correct.

    22×25×11=4×25×11=1,1002^2 \times 25 \times 11 = 4 \times 25 \times 11 = 1{,}10022×25×11=4×25×11=1,100

    But a prime factorization is a product of PRIMES, and 252525 is not one, so this is a tree with a branch left unfinished rather than a slip in the multiplication. Splitting that leaf gives 5×55 \times 55×5 and the finished form.

    1,100=22×52×111{,}100 = 2^2 \times 5^2 \times 111,100=22×52×11

    In one line

    The tree for 588588588 finishes at 22×3×722^2 \times 3 \times 7^222×3×72. Repeated division on 1,4521{,}4521,452 uses the divisors 222, 222, 333, 111111, 111111, justified by an even last digit for each 222, the digit sum 121212 for the 333, and division for each 111111, giving 22×3×1122^2 \times 3 \times 11^222×3×112. A tree has gone as far as it can exactly when every leaf is prime, and the raised number counts how many copies of that prime are multiplied together. The form 22×25×112^2 \times 25 \times 1122×25×11 multiplies back to 1,1001{,}1001,100 but is not a prime factorization, since 25=5×525 = 5 \times 525=5×5 is composite; repaired it reads 22×52×112^2 \times 5^2 \times 1122×52×11.

    4. Kits and reorders . 13 points. Question 4 of 10.

    13 pts

    A school supply room holds 110110110 pens and 154154154 notebooks. Pens are reordered every 121212 days and notebooks every 272727 days, and both orders were placed today.

    1. A
      Part A.

      The pens and notebooks are to be made up into identical kits, every kit holding the same number of pens and the same number of notebooks, with none left over and as many kits as possible. Give the number of kits and what one kit holds.

      Solve and show your work Write each step out, and end with the value and its units. 4 points

    2. B
      Part B.

      Give the number of days that pass before the two reorders next fall on the same day.

      Solve and show your work Write each step out, and end with the value and its units. 4 points

    3. C
      Part C.

      Each part above was settled by one of the two answers a pair of prime factorizations can give. Say which, and what in the wording chose it. Then give the value part A would have produced if the other one had been taken, and say why a supply room could not use it.

      Carry your own answer forward Argue from the two answers you produced in parts A and B, whatever they came to.

      Explain what it means Words, not just symbols. Say what the number is telling you about the situation. 5 points

    The answer

    Part A

    There are 222222 kits, each holding 555 pens and 777 notebooks.

    Part B

    108108108 days pass, which is 999 pen orders and 444 notebook orders.

    Part C

    Part A asks for the largest size fitting both stocks exactly, which takes the lowest power of each shared prime; part B asks when two cycles first coincide, which takes the highest power of every prime. The highest powers in part A give 770770770, more kits than there are pens, so no kit could be filled.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    Each kit takes an equal share of both stocks, so the number of kits divides 110110110 and also divides 154154154, and as many kits as possible means the greatest number that does both.

    110=2×5×11,154=2×7×11110 = 2 \times 5 \times 11, \qquad 154 = 2 \times 7 \times 11110=2×5×11,154=2×7×11

    The primes in both are 222 and 111111, each once in each number, and the lowest power of a shared prime is what a common factor may carry.

    GCF⁡(110,154)=2×11=22\operatorname{GCF}(110, 154) = 2 \times 11 = 22GCF(110,154)=2×11=22

    So there are 222222 kits, and each one holds 110÷22=5110 \div 22 = 5110÷22=5 pens and 154÷22=7154 \div 22 = 7154÷22=7 notebooks, with nothing left over.

    Part B

    Pen orders land on the multiples of 121212 and notebook orders on the multiples of 272727, so they fall together on a common multiple and NEXT fall together on the smallest one.

    12=22×3,27=3312 = 2^2 \times 3, \qquad 27 = 3^312=22×3,27=33

    A common multiple must hold enough copies of each prime for either cycle on its own, so take the highest power of each.

    LCM⁡(12,27)=22×33=108\operatorname{LCM}(12, 27) = 2^2 \times 3^3 = 108LCM(12,27)=22×33=108

    Checking, 108÷12=9108 \div 12 = 9108÷12=9 and 108÷27=4108 \div 27 = 4108÷27=4, both whole, so day 108108108 really is a day both orders are placed.

    Part C

    The two questions pull in opposite directions, and the wording says which way each pulls.

    Part A hands out a fixed stock, so its answer has to DIVIDE both totals, which caps every prime at the count held by the poorer number. That is the lowest power of each shared prime.

    GCF⁡(110,154)=22\operatorname{GCF}(110, 154) = 22GCF(110,154)=22

    Part B waits for two repeating cycles, so its answer has to be a MULTIPLE of both cycle lengths, which demands at least the count held by the richer number. That is the highest power of each prime.

    LCM⁡(12,27)=108\operatorname{LCM}(12, 27) = 108LCM(12,27)=108

    Taking the highest powers in part A instead would give a different number altogether.

    LCM⁡(110,154)=2×5×7×11=770\operatorname{LCM}(110, 154) = 2 \times 5 \times 7 \times 11 = 770LCM(110,154)=2×5×7×11=770

    A supply room cannot use 770770770 kits: there are only 110110110 pens, so most of the kits would stand empty. Whenever the answer to a sharing question comes out larger than the stock being shared, the two rules have been swapped.

    In one line

    The stocks make GCF⁡(110,154)=22\operatorname{GCF}(110, 154) = 22GCF(110,154)=22 kits, each holding 555 pens and 777 notebooks, and the two reorders next coincide after LCM⁡(12,27)=108\operatorname{LCM}(12, 27) = 108LCM(12,27)=108 days. Sharing a fixed stock asks for a number that divides both totals, so it takes the lowest power of each shared prime; waiting for two cycles to meet asks for a number both cycle lengths divide, so it takes the highest power of every prime. Taking the highest powers in part A would give 770770770, far more kits than there are pens to fill them.

    Rubric

    Mark your own paper against this. Give yourself the points for each element you actually wrote down, not the ones you meant to.

    Part A 4 points

    2

    Sets the number of kits up as a number dividing both stocks, and takes the greatest such number. . Worth 2 points.

    1

    1

    Part B 4 points

    2

    5. Where a test may be split . 14 points. Question 5 of 10.

    14 pts

    The number under test throughout is 7,8487{,}8487,848. Some divisors have a rule of their own, read off one block of digits, and some have no standalone rule taught in this chapter, so here they are tested by combining two taught rules.

    1. A
      Part A.

      Write 7,8487{,}8487,848 as a multiple of 100100100 plus the number made by its last two digits, and again as a multiple of 100010001000 plus the number made by its last three. Use those two splits to say why the test for 444 needs only two digits and the test for 888 only three.

      Complete the derivation Each line should follow from the one above it. Say what lets you take each step. 5 points

    2. B
      Part B.

      Say which of 444, 666, 888 and 999 divide 7,8487{,}8487,848, naming what each test reads.

      Solve and show your work Write each step out, and end with the value and its units. 4 points

    3. C
      Part C.

      A student proposes a general move: to test for any divisor, split it into two factors and run the tests for those two. Decide whether the move always works, taking 242424 split as 4×64 \times 64×6 as your case, and state the condition on the two factors that makes it sound.

      Justify your claim State the claim, then give the reason it has to be true. 5 points

    The answer

    Part A

    7,848=(78×100)+48=(7×1000)+8487{,}848 = (78 \times 100) + 48 = (7 \times 1000) + 8487,848=(78×100)+48=(7×1000)+848. Since 100=4×25100 = 4 \times 25100=4×25, the first piece is a multiple of 444 whatever stands above the last two digits, so only 484848 can decide that test; since 1000=8×1251000 = 8 \times 1251000=8×125, only 848848848 can decide the test for 888.

    Part B

    All four divide 7,8487{,}8487,848: the last two digits give 484848, the last three give 848848848, the digits add to 272727, and the number is even with that digit sum a multiple of 333.

    Part C

    The move is not always sound. 121212 passes the tests for 444 and for 666 and is not a multiple of 242424, because the two factors share a 222 that then gets counted twice. It is sound exactly when the two factors share no factor above 111, as 333 and 888 do not.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    Cut the numeral at the hundreds column, then at the thousands column.

    7,848=(78×100)+48,7,848=(7×1000)+8487{,}848 = (78 \times 100) + 48, \qquad 7{,}848 = (7 \times 1000) + 8487,848=(78×100)+48,7,848=(7×1000)+848

    In the first split the leading piece counts whole hundreds, and 100=4×25100 = 4 \times 25100=4×25, so that piece is 4×25×784 \times 25 \times 784×25×78: a multiple of 444, contributing remainder 000 however large the number is. If a sum of two pieces is being tested for 444 and one piece is already a multiple of 444, the verdict rests entirely on the other piece.

    48=4×1248 = 4 \times 1248=4×12

    So 7,8487{,}8487,848 is divisible by 444, and the digits above the last two never entered the argument. The second split works the same way one column out, because 1000=8×1251000 = 8 \times 1251000=8×125 makes the leading piece a multiple of 888.

    848=8×106848 = 8 \times 106848=8×106

    So 7,8487{,}8487,848 is divisible by 888 as well, decided by three digits. The reason the tests differ in length is exactly that 100100100 is a multiple of 444 but not of 888, while 100010001000 is a multiple of both.

    Part B

    Run the four tests, each on the part of the numeral it reads.

    48=4×12,848=8×106,7+8+4+8=27=9×348 = 4 \times 12, \qquad 848 = 8 \times 106, \qquad 7 + 8 + 4 + 8 = 27 = 9 \times 348=4×12,848=8×106,7+8+4+8=27=9×3

    The first two settle 444 and 888. The digit sum 272727 is a multiple of 999, so 999 divides the number, and since 272727 is also a multiple of 333 and the last digit 888 is even, the number passes both halves of the test for 666 as well.

    7,848÷6=1,3087{,}848 \div 6 = 1{,}3087,848÷6=1,308

    So every one of 444, 666, 888 and 999 divides 7,8487{,}8487,848.

    Part C

    Try the proposed split on a small number.

    12÷4=3,12÷6=2,12÷24 leaves a remainder12 \div 4 = 3, \qquad 12 \div 6 = 2, \qquad 12 \div 24 \text{ leaves a remainder}12÷4=3,12÷6=2,12÷24 leaves a remainder

    So 121212 passes both halves of the student's test for 242424 and is not a multiple of 242424: one counterexample is enough to sink the move as a general rule.

    The reason is that 444 and 666 overlap. Passing both tests puts two copies of 222 into the number (from the 444) and one copy of 222 with one copy of 333 (from the 666), but the single copy of 222 that the 666 demands may be one the 444 has already supplied. Nothing forces a third copy, and 24=23×324 = 2^3 \times 324=23×3 needs three.

    Split 242424 the other way and the overlap disappears.

    24=3×8,3 and 8 share no factor above 124 = 3 \times 8, \qquad 3 \text{ and } 8 \text{ share no factor above } 124=3×8,3 and 8 share no factor above 1

    Now the copies cannot be shared: the 888 supplies the three 222s and the 333 supplies the 333. So the move is sound exactly when the two factors have no common factor above 111, and 7,8487{,}8487,848, which passes the tests for 333 and 888, is indeed a multiple of 242424.

    In one line

    7,848=(78×100)+48=(7×1000)+8487{,}848 = (78 \times 100) + 48 = (7 \times 1000) + 8487,848=(78×100)+48=(7×1000)+848, and because 100=4×25100 = 4 \times 25100=4×25 and 1000=8×1251000 = 8 \times 1251000=8×125 the leading piece of each split contributes no remainder, so two digits settle the test for 444 and three settle the test for 888. All of 444, 666, 888 and 999 divide 7,8487{,}8487,848, its digit sum being 272727. Splitting a divisor into two factors and running their tests is sound only when those factors share no factor above 111: 121212 passes the tests for 444 and 666 without being a multiple of 242424, while the split 24=3×824 = 3 \times 824=3×8 carries no such overlap.

    6. One answer inside the other . 13 points. Question 6 of 10.

    13 pts

    For two whole numbers the greatest common factor and the least common multiple are not free of one another. Fix the two numbers and either answer settles the other.

    1. A
      Part A.

      Find GCF⁡(40,56)\operatorname{GCF}(40, 56)GCF(40,56) and LCM⁡(40,56)\operatorname{LCM}(40, 56)LCM(40,56) from their prime factorizations. Then multiply your two answers together, multiply 404040 by 565656, and compare the results.

      Solve and show your work Write each step out, and end with the value and its units. 4 points

    2. B
      Part B.

      Two whole numbers have a greatest common factor of 101010 and a least common multiple of 120120120. Give their product, and give a pair of numbers that fits, with neither of them equal to 101010.

      Solve and show your work Write each step out, and end with the value and its units. 4 points

    3. C
      Part C.

      Suppose one of two whole numbers divides the other. Say what the greatest common factor and the least common multiple must then be, and check the product rule against that case.

      Justify your claim State the claim, then give the reason it has to be true. 5 points

    The answer

    Part A

    GCF⁡(40,56)=8\operatorname{GCF}(40, 56) = 8GCF(40,56)=8 and LCM⁡(40,56)=280\operatorname{LCM}(40, 56) = 280LCM(40,56)=280. Both 8×2808 \times 2808×280 and 40×5640 \times 5640×56 come to 2,2402{,}2402,240.

    Part B

    Their product is 1,2001{,}2001,200, and the pair 303030 and 404040 fits.

    Part C

    The greatest common factor is the number that divides and the least common multiple is the other one. Multiplying the two answers is then multiplying the two numbers in the other order, so the rule holds with nothing left to check.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    Write both numbers in prime-power form.

    40=23×5,56=23×740 = 2^3 \times 5, \qquad 56 = 2^3 \times 740=23×5,56=23×7

    The only shared prime is 222, at three copies in each, so the lowest power is 232^323 and the greatest common factor is 888. For the least common multiple take the highest power of every prime that appears at all.

    LCM⁡(40,56)=23×5×7=280\operatorname{LCM}(40, 56) = 2^3 \times 5 \times 7 = 280LCM(40,56)=23×5×7=280

    Now multiply the two answers, and multiply the two numbers.

    8×280=2,240,40×56=2,2408 \times 280 = 2{,}240, \qquad 40 \times 56 = 2{,}2408×280=2,240,40×56=2,240

    The two agree, as they must: between them the answers take the lower and the higher count of every prime, which is the pair of counts over again.

    Part B

    The two answers multiply back to the two numbers multiplied together, so the product is fixed even though the numbers are not yet known.

    10×120=1,20010 \times 120 = 1{,}20010×120=1,200

    To find a pair, note that both numbers are multiples of 101010, say 10×u10 \times u10×u and 10×v10 \times v10×v, and their product must be 1,2001{,}2001,200, so u×v=12u \times v = 12u×v=12. Take uuu and vvv sharing no factor above 111, or the greatest common factor would climb past 101010.

    u=3,  v=4  ⇒  30 and 40u = 3, \; v = 4 \;\Rightarrow\; 30 \text{ and } 40u=3,v=4⇒30 and 40

    Checking, 30=2×3×530 = 2 \times 3 \times 530=2×3×5 and 40=23×540 = 2^3 \times 540=23×5, so the greatest common factor is 2×5=102 \times 5 = 102×5=10 and the least common multiple is 23×3×5=1202^3 \times 3 \times 5 = 12023×3×5=120.

    Part C

    Let the smaller number divide the larger. The smaller divides itself and it divides the larger, so it is a common factor, and no common factor can exceed the smaller number, so it is the greatest one. The larger is a multiple of itself and a multiple of the smaller, so it is a common multiple, and no common multiple can be below the larger number, so it is the least one.

    GCF⁡(40,120)=40,LCM⁡(40,120)=120\operatorname{GCF}(40, 120) = 40, \qquad \operatorname{LCM}(40, 120) = 120GCF(40,120)=40,LCM(40,120)=120

    The two answers are therefore the two numbers over again, and the product rule becomes an identity.

    40×120=40×12040 \times 120 = 40 \times 12040×120=40×120

    The prime powers say the same thing: if one number divides the other, then at every prime its count is the lower one, so one number supplies every lowest power and the other supplies every highest power.

    In one line

    GCF⁡(40,56)=8\operatorname{GCF}(40, 56) = 8GCF(40,56)=8 and LCM⁡(40,56)=280\operatorname{LCM}(40, 56) = 280LCM(40,56)=280, and 8×280=40×56=2,2408 \times 280 = 40 \times 56 = 2{,}2408×280=40×56=2,240. Two numbers with a greatest common factor of 101010 and a least common multiple of 120120120 must have product 1,2001{,}2001,200, and 303030 and 404040 is such a pair. When one number divides the other, the greatest common factor is the number that divides and the least common multiple is the other one, so the product rule reduces to multiplying the two numbers in the other order.

    7. A number given only by its primes . 13 points. Question 7 of 10.

    13 pts

    Two whole numbers are written out as prime powers: N=23×32×11N = 2^3 \times 3^2 \times 11N=23×32×11 and M=22×5×7M = 2^2 \times 5 \times 7M=22×5×7. Nothing here needs multiplying out, because the exponents are the whole record of what each number is made of.

    1. A
      Part A.

      Decide for each of 181818, 333333 and 202020 whether it is a factor of NNN, giving your reason in terms of the copies of each prime.

      Write the expression An equation or an expression is enough here. Show how you built it. 4 points

    2. B
      Part B.

      Give the prime factorization of N×MN \times MN×M in prime-power form, and say how many copies of the prime 222 it holds.

      Write the expression An equation or an expression is enough here. Show how you built it. 4 points

    3. C
      Part C.

      Two students argue about NNN. One says every whole number greater than 111 that divides NNN has to be one of 222, 333 and 111111. The other says no prime outside 222, 333 and 111111 can divide NNN. Decide each claim.

      Carry your own answer forward You may use your conclusions from part A, whatever they were.

      Justify your claim State the claim, then give the reason it has to be true. 5 points

    The answer

    Part A

    181818 and 333333 are factors of NNN. 202020 is not, because it asks for a copy of the prime 555 and NNN holds none.

    Part B

    N×M=25×32×5×7×11N \times M = 2^5 \times 3^2 \times 5 \times 7 \times 11N×M=25×32×5×7×11, which holds five copies of the prime 222.

    Part C

    The first is wrong: 666 divides NNN and is none of the three, since a factor may be built from several of the primes at once. The second is right: a prime dividing NNN would have to appear in the single factorization NNN has, and only 222, 333 and 111111 appear there.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    A number divides NNN exactly when every prime it asks for is present in NNN in at least the quantity it asks for. So factor each candidate and compare tallies.

    18=2×32,33=3×11,20=22×518 = 2 \times 3^2, \qquad 33 = 3 \times 11, \qquad 20 = 2^2 \times 518=2×32,33=3×11,20=22×5

    Against N=23×32×11N = 2^3 \times 3^2 \times 11N=23×32×11: the first asks for one 222 and two 333s, and NNN has three 222s and two 333s, so it fits; the second asks for one 333 and one 111111, and both are there, so it fits too.

    The third asks for a copy of 555. Nothing in NNN can supply it, because NNN has exactly one prime factorization and 555 does not appear in it, so 202020 is not a factor.

    Part B

    Multiplying two numbers sets their factorizations side by side, so counting a prime inside the product means adding the two counts. The prime 222 appears three times in NNN and twice in MMM.

    N×M=(23×32×11)×(22×5×7)N \times M = (2^3 \times 3^2 \times 11) \times (2^2 \times 5 \times 7)N×M=(23×32×11)×(22×5×7)

    Gathering equal primes and listing them from smallest to largest,

    N×M=25×32×5×7×11N \times M = 2^5 \times 3^2 \times 5 \times 7 \times 11N×M=25×32×5×7×11

    so the product holds five copies of 222. Every other prime appears in only one of the two numbers, so it enters the product at the power it already had.

    Part C

    The two claims sound alike and are not, because one is about factors and the other about PRIME factors.

    The first is false, and one factor settles it.

    6=2×3,N=6×(22×3×11)6 = 2 \times 3, \qquad N = 6 \times (2^2 \times 3 \times 11)6=2×3,N=6×(22×3×11)

    So 666 divides NNN without being one of the three primes. A factor may be assembled from any of the copies NNN owns, and 444, 999, 222222 and 333333 divide NNN for the same reason.

    The second is true, and uniqueness is what makes it true. Suppose a prime ppp divided NNN, so that N=p×kN = p \times kN=p×k for some whole number kkk. Factoring kkk into primes and putting ppp in front produces a prime factorization of NNN that contains ppp. But NNN has exactly one prime factorization apart from order, and the one it has is 23×32×112^3 \times 3^2 \times 1123×32×11, so ppp has to be 222, 333 or 111111.

    That is the whole use of the theorem here: a prime cannot hide inside a number without showing up in its factorization.

    In one line

    Of the three candidates, 18=2×3218 = 2 \times 3^218=2×32 and 33=3×1133 = 3 \times 1133=3×11 divide NNN, while 20=22×520 = 2^2 \times 520=22×5 does not, since NNN holds no copy of 555. Multiplying adds the prime counts, so N×M=25×32×5×7×11N \times M = 2^5 \times 3^2 \times 5 \times 7 \times 11N×M=25×32×5×7×11, with five copies of 222. The first student is wrong, because 666 divides NNN and is not one of its primes; the second is right, because a prime dividing NNN would have to appear in the one prime factorization NNN has.

    8. What a third number changes . 14 points. Question 8 of 10.

    14 pts

    Three whole numbers are on the table: 303030, 424242 and 707070. The parts below ask for the two answers a set of prime factorizations gives, and then for what becomes of them when the list gets shorter.

    1. A
      Part A.

      Write each of the three numbers in prime-power form, then give GCF⁡(30,42,70)\operatorname{GCF}(30, 42, 70)GCF(30,42,70) and LCM⁡(30,42,70)\operatorname{LCM}(30, 42, 70)LCM(30,42,70).

      Write the expression An equation or an expression is enough here. Show how you built it. 5 points

    2. B
      Part B.

      Now drop 707070 from the list. Give the greatest common factor and the least common multiple of the two numbers left, and say for each answer whether it rose, fell or stayed.

      Carry your own answer forward Compare the two answers here with the pair you produced in part A, whatever they came to.

      Solve and show your work Write each step out, and end with the value and its units. 4 points

    3. C
      Part C.

      Explain why dropping a number can never lower a greatest common factor or raise a least common multiple, and account for what each of your two answers did.

      Carry your own answer forward Account for the change, or the lack of one, between your own answers in parts A and B.

      Explain why it works A sentence or two. Reasons, not steps. 5 points

    The answer

    Part A

    30=2×3×530 = 2 \times 3 \times 530=2×3×5, 42=2×3×742 = 2 \times 3 \times 742=2×3×7 and 70=2×5×770 = 2 \times 5 \times 770=2×5×7, so GCF⁡=2\operatorname{GCF} = 2GCF=2 and LCM⁡=210\operatorname{LCM} = 210LCM=210.

    Part B

    For 303030 and 424242 the greatest common factor is 666, which has risen, and the least common multiple is 210210210, which has stayed where it was.

    Part C

    A common factor of fewer numbers has fewer conditions to meet, so the greatest common factor can only rise or stay; a common multiple of fewer numbers faces fewer demands, so the least common multiple can only fall or stay. It stayed at 210210210 because 424242 still supplies the 777 and 303030 still supplies the 555.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    Take the three factorizations first.

    30=2×3×5,42=2×3×7,70=2×5×730 = 2 \times 3 \times 5, \qquad 42 = 2 \times 3 \times 7, \qquad 70 = 2 \times 5 \times 730=2×3×5,42=2×3×7,70=2×5×7

    For the greatest common factor, keep only the primes every one of the three owns, each at its lowest power. The prime 333 is missing from 707070, the prime 555 from 424242 and the prime 777 from 303030, so all three drop out and only 222 survives.

    GCF⁡(30,42,70)=2\operatorname{GCF}(30, 42, 70) = 2GCF(30,42,70)=2

    For the least common multiple, take the highest power of every prime that appears anywhere.

    LCM⁡(30,42,70)=2×3×5×7=210\operatorname{LCM}(30, 42, 70) = 2 \times 3 \times 5 \times 7 = 210LCM(30,42,70)=2×3×5×7=210

    Both ends check: 222 divides all three, and 210÷30=7210 \div 30 = 7210÷30=7, 210÷42=5210 \div 42 = 5210÷42=5, 210÷70=3210 \div 70 = 3210÷70=3.

    Part B

    With 707070 gone, only 303030 and 424242 have a say.

    30=2×3×5,42=2×3×730 = 2 \times 3 \times 5, \qquad 42 = 2 \times 3 \times 730=2×3×5,42=2×3×7

    The primes in both are now 222 and 333, each once in each number, so the greatest common factor picks up a factor it could not have before.

    GCF⁡(30,42)=2×3=6\operatorname{GCF}(30, 42) = 2 \times 3 = 6GCF(30,42)=2×3=6

    That has risen from 222, because 707070 was the number holding no copy of 333. For the least common multiple, the highest powers are unchanged.

    LCM⁡(30,42)=2×3×5×7=210\operatorname{LCM}(30, 42) = 2 \times 3 \times 5 \times 7 = 210LCM(30,42)=2×3×5×7=210

    That is where it already was.

    Part C

    Think of each number in the list as imposing conditions, prime by prime.

    A common factor must fit inside every number on the list, so each number caps how many copies of a prime the factor may carry. Removing a number removes caps and never adds one, so everything that was a common factor still is, and there may be more besides. The greatest of a larger collection cannot be smaller, so the answer rises or stays.

    A common multiple must cover every number on the list, so each number sets a floor under how many copies of a prime the multiple must hold. Removing a number removes a floor and never adds one, so everything that was a common multiple still is, and the least of a larger collection cannot be larger.

    Here the caps were what moved. The number 707070 holds no copy of 333, so while it was on the list no common factor could carry a 333; once it went, the 333 that 303030 and 424242 both own became available.

    2⟶2×3=62 \longrightarrow 2 \times 3 = 62⟶2×3=6

    The floors did not move at all, because no prime had its highest count held by 707070 alone.

    5 sits in 30,7 sits in 425 \text{ sits in } 30, \qquad 7 \text{ sits in } 425 sits in 30,7 sits in 42

    Every prime that 707070 demanded was already demanded by one of the other two, at the same power, so the least common multiple had nothing to give up and stayed at 210210210.

    In one line

    From 30=2×3×530 = 2 \times 3 \times 530=2×3×5, 42=2×3×742 = 2 \times 3 \times 742=2×3×7 and 70=2×5×770 = 2 \times 5 \times 770=2×5×7, the greatest common factor is 222 and the least common multiple is 210210210. Dropping 707070 raises the greatest common factor to 666 and leaves the least common multiple at 210210210. A shorter list caps a common factor less and demands less of a common multiple, so the first answer can only rise or stay and the second can only fall or stay; here the second stayed because 303030 still supplies the 555 and 424242 still supplies the 777 that 707070 had been contributing.

    9. Two numbers under trial division . 15 points. Question 9 of 10.

    15 pts

    Trial division settles a number in one of two ways: it turns up a factor, or it runs out of candidates. Where it runs out is fixed by the number itself, not by how many divisions have already failed.

    1. A
      Part A.

      Decide whether 337337337 is prime, saying which candidate divisors you tried and showing that your search went far enough to settle it.

      Solve and show your work Write each step out, and end with the value and its units. 5 points

    2. B
      Part B.

      Decide whether 611611611 is prime, naming the divisor that settles it if there is one.

      Solve and show your work Write each step out, and end with the value and its units. 5 points

    3. C
      Part C.

      A classmate tries 222, 333, 555, 777 and 111111 on 611611611, finds no factor, and stops there, saying that five failed divisions in a row are enough to settle it. Say what the stopping rule actually permits, whether this stop was permitted, and what it would take to complete the search.

      Carry your own answer forward Judge the classmate against your own search in part B, whichever candidates you tried and whatever verdict you reached.

      Find and correct the error Say which line first goes wrong, why it is wrong, and then do it correctly. 5 points

    The answer

    Part A

    337337337 is prime. The obliged candidates are 222, 333, 555, 777, 111111, 131313 and 171717, and 191919 is the first that may be skipped.

    Part B

    611611611 is composite. The divisor 131313 settles it, since 611=13×47611 = 13 \times 47611=13×47.

    Part C

    Five failed divisions settle nothing. The search may stop only once a candidate times itself passes the number, and 13×13=16913 \times 13 = 16913×13=169 is far below 611611611, so 131313 was still owed. It divides, giving 611=13×47611 = 13 \times 47611=13×47, so the classmate has called a composite number prime.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    Test candidates while the candidate times itself does not pass the number.

    17×17=289≤337,19×19=361>33717 \times 17 = 289 \le 337, \qquad 19 \times 19 = 361 > 33717×17=289≤337,19×19=361>337

    So the obliged list runs 222, 333, 555, 777, 111111, 131313, 171717, and 191919 is the first candidate the stopping rule excuses. The quick tests clear the first three: 337337337 is odd, its digits add to 131313, and it does not end in 000 or 555. The rest need division.

    337=(7×48)+1=(11×30)+7=(13×25)+12=(17×19)+14337 = (7 \times 48) + 1 = (11 \times 30) + 7 = (13 \times 25) + 12 = (17 \times 19) + 14337=(7×48)+1=(11×30)+7=(13×25)+12=(17×19)+14

    Every one leaves a remainder, so no factor pair exists and 337337337 is prime.

    Part B

    The quick tests all fail: 611611611 is odd, its digits add to 888, and it does not end in 000 or 555. So the search moves up through the candidates.

    611=(7×87)+2,611=(11×55)+6611 = (7 \times 87) + 2, \qquad 611 = (11 \times 55) + 6611=(7×87)+2,611=(11×55)+6

    Neither fits, and the next candidate is 131313.

    611÷13=47611 \div 13 = 47611÷13=47

    That is a third factor besides 111 and 611611611, so the number is composite and the search can stop the moment it appears.

    Part C

    The rule is not about how many divisions have failed. It is about where the factor pairs can still be hiding.

    24×24=576≤611,25×25=625>61124 \times 24 = 576 \le 611, \qquad 25 \times 25 = 625 > 61124×24=576≤611,25×25=625>611

    So every candidate up to 242424 is owed, which means the primes 222, 333, 555, 777, 111111, 131313, 171717, 191919 and 232323. The classmate stopped after five of the nine.

    What the rule guarantees is that the smaller partner of any factor pair is small enough that multiplying it by itself does not pass the number. Stopping early throws that guarantee away: a factor pair whose smaller partner is 131313, 171717, 191919 or 232323 would go unseen.

    611=13×47611 = 13 \times 47611=13×47

    The very next candidate was the one that worked, so the stop cost the whole verdict: the classmate would report a composite number as prime. A run of failed divisions is evidence of nothing on its own, since every composite number fails a great many divisions before the one that succeeds.

    In one line

    337337337 is prime: the obliged candidates are 222, 333, 555, 777, 111111, 131313 and 171717, since 17×17=28917 \times 17 = 28917×17=289 does not pass 337337337 while 19×19=36119 \times 19 = 36119×19=361 does, and every one of them leaves a remainder. 611611611 is composite, settled by 131313, since 611=13×47611 = 13 \times 47611=13×47. The classmate's stop after five failed divisions is not permitted: the rule ends the search only once a candidate times itself passes the number, which for 611611611 means going as far as 232323, and the very next candidate, 131313, was the one that divides.

    Rubric

    Mark your own paper against this. Give yourself the points for each element you actually wrote down, not the ones you meant to.
