  10. 10

    10. Carrying a rule to a third number . 15 points. Question 10 of 10.

    15 pts

    For two whole numbers, the greatest common factor and the least common multiple multiply back to the two numbers multiplied together. The parts below put that rule to work on a pair, and then on a set of three.

    1. A
      Part A.

      For 454545 and 606060, give the greatest common factor and the least common multiple, and check that the two answers multiply to 45×6045 \times 6045×60.

      Solve and show your work Write each step out, and end with the value and its units. 4 points

    2. B
      Part B.

      Now bring in a third number, 505050. Give GCF⁡(45,50,60)\operatorname{GCF}(45, 50, 60)GCF(45,50,60) and LCM⁡(45,50,60)\operatorname{LCM}(45, 50, 60)LCM(45,50,60), multiply those two answers together, and compare the result with 45×50×6045 \times 50 \times 6045×50×60.

      Solve and show your work Write each step out, and end with the value and its units. 5 points

    3. C
      Part C.

      The rule for two numbers turns on a pair of counts holding nothing but a lower one and a higher one. Using the prime 555 in part B as your case, account for the comparison you reached there. Then decide a classmate's claim that for three numbers the two answers can never multiply to the product.

      Carry your own answer forward Argue from the counts in the three factorizations you wrote in part B, whatever answers they gave you.

      Justify your claim State the claim, then give the reason it has to be true. 6 points

    The answer

    Part A

    GCF⁡(45,60)=15\operatorname{GCF}(45, 60) = 15GCF(45,60)=15 and LCM⁡(45,60)=180\operatorname{LCM}(45, 60) = 180LCM(45,60)=180, and 15×180=45×60=2,70015 \times 180 = 45 \times 60 = 2{,}70015×180=45×60=2,700.

    Part B

    GCF⁡(45,50,60)=5\operatorname{GCF}(45, 50, 60) = 5GCF(45,50,60)=5 and LCM⁡(45,50,60)=900\operatorname{LCM}(45, 50, 60) = 900LCM(45,50,60)=900, so the two answers give 4,5004{,}5004,500, while 45×50×60=135,00045 \times 50 \times 60 = 135{,}00045×50×60=135,000. The two are not equal.

    Part C

    A third count sits between the lowest and the highest, and neither answer reaches for it: at the prime 555 the counts are 111, 222 and 111, so the two answers collect three copies where the product holds four. The claim is still wrong: 555, 888 and 999 share no prime, and 1×360=5×8×91 \times 360 = 5 \times 8 \times 91×360=5×8×9.

    Worked solution

    Part A

    Write both in prime-power form and go prime by prime.

    45=32×5,60=22×3×545 = 3^2 \times 5, \qquad 60 = 2^2 \times 3 \times 545=32×5,60=22×3×5

    The shared primes are 333 and 555. Lowest powers give the greatest common factor, highest powers give the least common multiple.

    GCF⁡(45,60)=3×5=15,LCM⁡(45,60)=22×32×5=180\operatorname{GCF}(45, 60) = 3 \times 5 = 15, \qquad \operatorname{LCM}(45, 60) = 2^2 \times 3^2 \times 5 = 180GCF(45,60)=3×5=15,LCM(45,60)=22×32×5=180

    Now multiply each pair.

    15×180=2,700,45×60=2,70015 \times 180 = 2{,}700, \qquad 45 \times 60 = 2{,}70015×180=2,700,45×60=2,700

    They agree, because at every prime the two answers take the lower count and the higher count, and a pair of counts holds nothing else.

    Part B

    Add the third factorization and run both rules across all three columns.

    45=32×5,50=2×52,60=22×3×545 = 3^2 \times 5, \qquad 50 = 2 \times 5^2, \qquad 60 = 2^2 \times 3 \times 545=32×5,50=2×52,60=22×3×5

    Only 555 sits in all three, at one copy in the poorest of them, so that is the whole of the greatest common factor. For the least common multiple take the highest power of each prime anywhere: 222^222 from 606060, 323^232 from 454545 and 525^252 from 505050.

    GCF⁡=5,LCM⁡=22×32×52=900\operatorname{GCF} = 5, \qquad \operatorname{LCM} = 2^2 \times 3^2 \times 5^2 = 900GCF=5,LCM=22×32×52=900

    Now set the two products side by side.

    5×900=4,500,45×50×60=135,0005 \times 900 = 4{,}500, \qquad 45 \times 50 \times 60 = 135{,}0005×900=4,500,45×50×60=135,000

    They are not equal, and not even close: the product is 303030 times the other.

    Part C

    With two numbers, sorting a pair of counts changes nothing about what the pair holds, so the lower and the higher between them use the pair up, and the two answers hold exactly as many copies of each prime as the product does. Three counts have a middle one, and neither answer ever reaches for it.

    Watch the prime 555 across the three numbers of part B. It appears once in 454545, twice in 505050 and once in 606060.

    lowest 1,middle 1,highest 2\text{lowest } 1, \quad \text{middle } 1, \quad \text{highest } 2lowest 1,middle 1,highest 2

    The greatest common factor takes one copy and the least common multiple takes two, three in all, while the product 45×50×6045 \times 50 \times 6045×50×60 holds 1+2+1=41 + 2 + 1 = 41+2+1=4. One copy of 555 goes uncollected. The primes 222 and 333 each lose a copy the same way, which is exactly the factor of 303030 separating 4,5004{,}5004,500 from 135,000135{,}000135,000.

    The classmate's claim goes too far, though. Nothing is lost when there is no middle copy to lose, and that happens whenever no two of the three numbers share a prime.

    5=5,8=23,9=325 = 5, \qquad 8 = 2^3, \qquad 9 = 3^25=5,8=23,9=32

    Here the greatest common factor is 111 and the least common multiple is 23×32×5=3602^3 \times 3^2 \times 5 = 36023×32×5=360, which is the product itself, so the two answers do multiply to 5×8×9=3605 \times 8 \times 9 = 3605×8×9=360. The honest statement is that there is no RULE of that shape for three numbers, not that it always fails.

    In one line

    For 454545 and 606060 the answers are 151515 and 180180180, and 15×180=45×60=2,70015 \times 180 = 45 \times 60 = 2{,}70015×180=45×60=2,700. Bringing in 505050 gives 555 and 900900900, whose product 4,5004{,}5004,500 falls well short of 45×50×60=135,00045 \times 50 \times 60 = 135{,}00045×50×60=135,000, because a third number contributes a middle count at each prime that neither answer collects: at the prime 555 the counts are 111, 111 and 222, so three copies are collected where the product holds four. The classmate goes too far all the same, since 555, 888 and 999 share no prime and give 1×360=5×8×91 \times 360 = 5 \times 8 \times 91×360=5×8×9.

    Rubric

    Mark your own paper against this. Give yourself the points for each element you actually wrote down, not the ones you meant to.

    2

    Finds both answers from the prime powers, taking lowest powers for one and highest for the other. . Worth 2 points.

    2

    Carries out both multiplications and reports that they agree. . Worth 2 points.

    Part B 5 points

    2

    Applies both rules across all three numbers, dropping from the greatest common factor every prime that any one of them lacks. . Worth 2 points.

    2

    Reaches 555 and 900900900, and multiplies them out. . Worth 2 points.

    1

    Compares the two results and states plainly that they differ. . Worth 1 point.

    Part C 6 points

    3

    Identifies the middle count as what neither answer collects, and tracks it at the prime 555 through the counts 111, 111 and 222. . Worth 3 points. needs an explanation, not just an answer

    3

    Rejects the classmate's claim and exhibits three numbers, no two sharing a prime, for which the two answers do multiply to the product. . Worth 3 points. needs an explanation, not just an answer
